The central question is: when you merge two fine-tuned models via task arithmetic (adding or subtracting their weight-space deltas), does interference between tasks localize to specific layers or parameter subsets, and does that localization pattern depend on whether the fine-tuning updates happened to land in overlapping versus orthogonal subspaces of the weight matrix? Task arithmetic assumes interference is roughly uniform or ignorable, but the real concern is that two fine-tuned models from the same base family (e.g., both derived from Llama-3-8B) share not just initialization but implicit inductive biases that push their LoRA or full fine-tuning updates into functionally similar subspaces — meaning the delta vectors aren't random, they're correlated by architecture, and those correlations produce structured, not random, interference.

The key concepts are: (1) task vectors — the delta between fine-tuned and base weights; (2) subspace overlap — measured by principal angles between the column spaces of the two delta matrices; (3) interference localization — whether destructive superposition concentrates in attention heads, MLP blocks, or specific layers; and (4) functional adjacency — the idea that models trained on semantically related tasks (say, summarization and instruction-following) will have deltas that are geometrically closer in weight space than models trained on unrelated tasks.

What a beginner misses is that "non-orthogonal" doesn't just mean the merge is noisier — it means the interference has structure you can exploit or be burned by. If both fine-tunings strongly activate the same singular vectors in layer 12's MLP, merging amplifies those directions unpredictably (sometimes constructively for one task, destructively for the other), and naively scaling the task vector coefficient doesn't fix this because you're scaling signal and interference together. The expert worry is that standard evaluation benchmarks won't catch this: a merged model can score well on held-out task metrics while having silently destroyed narrow but critical capabilities (e.g., a specific reasoning chain type) that only show up in adversarial or out-of-distribution probing.

The critical experimental control is to also run random rotation of one task vector before merging as a null: if rotating into an artificially orthogonal subspace recovers performance, you've confirmed the interference is subspace-driven rather than magnitude-driven. The non-obvious confound an expert would flag is that LoRA constrains deltas to rank-r subspaces by construction, so you're not measuring natural fine-tuning geometry — you're measuring the geometry of a projection, and two LoRA models with identical underlying task updates but different random initializations of their A matrices will show artificially low subspace overlap despite being functionally identical updates.

A post-hoc alignment alternative is to use CKA (Centered Kernel Alignment) between the activation spaces induced by each fine-tuned model on a shared probe dataset, rather than comparing weight deltas directly — this sidesteps parameterization entirely because two adapters with different A initializations but identical functional updates will produce identical CKA scores, and Nguyen et al. showed CKA is robust to orthogonal transformation of representations. A more surgical procedure is Procrustes alignment of the singular subspaces: compute SVD of ΔW₁ and ΔW₂, then find the orthogonal matrix Q minimizing ||U₁ - U₂Q||_F — the residual after optimal alignment is your true task overlap metric, purged of rotation ambiguity from initialization. The strongest candidate is DARE (Delta-compression with Random Dropping) combined with high-rank LoRA (r=128 or r=256), where you train a fat adapter and then sparsify the reconstructed ΔW — this gets you a delta matrix whose singular value spectrum more closely resembles full fine-tuning's heavy-tailed distribution rather than LoRA's artificially truncated rank-r spectrum, which is the geometric property that actually matters for merge behavior. A third option worth considering is Flora or similar approaches that use random projections to compress optimizer states rather than the weight updates themselves, allowing full-rank weight updates at reduced memory cost — at 70B scale with aggressive quantization of optimizer states (as in 8-bit Adam), full fine-tuning of selected layers (say, only MLP down-projection matrices) is now feasible on 8×H100 clusters and gives you ground-truth geometry for those layers. To verify approximation quality, you'd measure two things: (1) the spectral divergence between the singular value distributions of ΔW_peft and ΔW_full on a smaller proxy model (e.g., Llama-3-8B) where you can afford both, using KL divergence on the normalized singular value spectra; and (2) merge fidelity transfer — whether the rank-ordering of task pair mergeability (which pairs interfere most) is preserved between the PEFT and full fine-tuning regimes on the proxy, then bet that the ordering holds at 70B. The underappreciated verification trap is that a PEFT method can match full fine-tuning's aggregate spectral statistics while still misaligning the top singular vectors specifically — and it's the top-3 to top-10 singular vectors that dominate interference in task arithmetic, so you need per-vector alignment checks (principal angles between top-k subspaces), not just distributional similarity.
